doc.title: Ruth & Bucky Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Saddle River, New Jersey, January 19, 2015

title: Learning songs by composer and keys of the Great American Songbook
summary: Bucky explains learning repertoire by composer, and why sheet music appears in flat or easier keys.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Yeah, that’s part of the — how did you learn all those songs that you know?
Number one, I can fake a lot of them. You know what I mean?
If you’re playing the piano and I have to follow you I can do it.
Okay. But somebody needs to know, right? Hopefully the bass player, right?

Yeah I have to know the songs — I learn the songs according to the composers. You get all the Richard Rodgers songs and you see hey he wrote this, he wrote that, then you build a repertoire. That’s the way I learned it.
Do you have an opinion why most of the songs like from the Great American Songbook are in flat keys?
No, I don’t know why. Well it might be when they sell sheet music it’s easier to have something that’s written in the key of F than it is in the key of F sharp.
True. Who wants to play that, right?
A person picks up the music and goes, “naaa”.

Well if you look at “Stardust” it’s in D flat, the original key, that’s five flats. But when you buy the music sometimes it’s written in C. Then the fake books come out and some wise guy puts some different chords in there that don’t fit.
